name: overlay-arrow
title: OverlayArrow
description: The marker that points from a floating panel back at the thing that opened it.

files.content:
import { OverlayArrow as AriaOverlayArrow } from 'react-aria-components'
import type { OverlayArrowProps as AriaOverlayArrowProps } from 'react-aria-components'

/**
 * The shape of the marker: a rotated square with two hairlines and the panel's own fill, so it continues
 * the panel's edge out to a point. Every other surface here is squared; an SVG arrow would be the one
 * curved thing in the system.
 *
 * **The rotation is on the shape inside React Aria's element, not on the element itself.** That element is
 * positioned with an inline `transform`, and an inline style outranks every class — a `rotate-45` written
 * on it type-checks, looks right in the source, and does nothing at all. The first version of this file did
 * exactly that and rendered an unrotated square sitting on the panel's edge.
 *
 * The two edges facing outward are the ones kept, so the other two disappear under the panel. Which two
 * depends on where React Aria put the overlay, which it reports as `data-placement` on the **parent** —
 * hence the arbitrary ancestor variants rather than plain `data-[…]` ones.
 */
export const OVERLAY_ARROW = [
  'block size-2 rotate-45 border-border-strong bg-card',
  '[[data-placement=bottom]_&]:border-t [[data-placement=bottom]_&]:border-l',
  '[[data-placement=top]_&]:border-r [[data-placement=top]_&]:border-b',
  '[[data-placement=left]_&]:border-t [[data-placement=left]_&]:border-r',
  '[[data-placement=right]_&]:border-b [[data-placement=right]_&]:border-l',
].join(' ')

/** React Aria positions this element; all it needs from us is to stay above the panel. */
export const OVERLAY_ARROW_POSITION = 'z-10'

/**
 * The marker that points from a floating panel back at the thing that opened it.
 *
 * ```tsx
 * <Popover>
 *   <Popover.Arrow />
 *   …
 * </Popover>
 * ```
 *
 * **Nothing here uses one by default, and that is a decision rather than an oversight.** A pointer is a
 * shape the design language does not otherwise contain: the sheet's panels are flat rectangles joined to
 * their trigger by proximity and position, and every menu, select and tooltip in this system opens
 * anchored without one. So it is an opt-in slot — `Popover.Arrow`, `Tooltip.Arrow` — for the case where a
 * panel must be tied to a small target and proximity is not enough.
 *
 * React Aria positions this element and reports which way it must point as `data-placement`.
 */
export interface OverlayArrowProps extends Omit<
  AriaOverlayArrowProps,
  'className'
> {
  className?: string
}

export function OverlayArrow({ className, ...props }: OverlayArrowProps) {
  return (
    <AriaOverlayArrow
      data-slot="overlay-arrow"
      className={OVERLAY_ARROW_POSITION}
      {...props}
    >
      <span
        data-slot="overlay-arrow-shape"
        className={[OVERLAY_ARROW, className].filter(Boolean).join(' ')}
      />
    </AriaOverlayArrow>
  )
}

The marker that points from a floating panel back at the thing that opened it. ```tsx

Anchored to the button.

 ``` | Slot | React Aria | Notes | | --------------- | -------------- | ---------------------------------- | | `Popover.Arrow` | `OverlayArrow` | Opt-in; inside the popover | | `Tooltip.Arrow` | `OverlayArrow` | Opt-in; inside the tooltip content | ## Nothing uses one by default, and that is a decision A pointer is a shape the design language does not otherwise contain. The sheet's panels are flat rectangles joined to their trigger by proximity and position, and every menu, select and tooltip here opens anchored without one — so it is neither in `popover.ts` nor built into `Popover`. It was left out for three rounds on **inference**, which is a weak reason. Building it as an **opt-in slot** settles the question with code instead: if nothing uses it, the judgement is confirmed; if something needs it, it is already there. That is the difference between a decision and a guess. ## A rotated square, not a triangle ```tsx // The shape's own class list, and the reason it is a separate element: 'block size-2 rotate-45 border-border-strong bg-card' '[[data-placement=bottom]_&]:border-t [[data-placement=bottom]_&]:border-l' ``` Two hairlines and the panel's own fill continue the panel's edge out to a point — the same squared geometry as every other surface here. An SVG arrow would be the one curved thing in the system. Which two edges are kept depends on where React Aria put the overlay, reported as `data-placement` on the **parent** — hence arbitrary ancestor variants rather than plain `data-[…]` ones. ## Two things that cost a round **React Aria owns the outer element's `transform`.** It positions the arrow with an inline `transform`, and an inline style outranks every class — so a `rotate-45` written on that element type-checks, reads correctly in the source, and does nothing. The first version did exactly that and drew an unrotated square. The rotation lives on a `` inside it. This is the third time in this repo an inline style has silently beaten a class. **Tailwind v4 writes the `rotate` property, not `transform`.** The assertion that caught the first bug then reported `transform: 'none'` for an element that _was_ visibly rotated, because `rotate-45` sets `rotate: 45deg`. The code was right and the assertion was wrong. Check `rotate`. ## Focus is the reliable way into a tooltip `Tooltip.Arrow`'s story focuses the trigger with `tab()` rather than hovering it. A tooltip must open for a keyboard user with no pointer, so focus is the first-class route — and it is also the one that does not depend on a hover delay.
